title: Astronomers Spot First Green “Zombie” Star Just in Time for Halloween 🎃✨
body:
Astronomers have identified the first known “green” star—a white dwarf whose atmosphere contains sodium that absorbs orange light, leaving a spectral signature that glows a haunting emerald hue. The discovery, made using high‑resolution spectroscopy of a distant, cooling stellar remnant, adds a new twist to our understanding of how dying stars evolve and how exotic chemistry can shape the appearance of celestial objects. The timing of the find, announced just weeks before Halloween, has sparked playful comparisons to a cosmic zombie, but the science behind the phenomenon is anything but fiction.

The object, catalogued as WD J2105‑0722, lies roughly 400 light‑years from Earth and belongs to the class of white dwarfs known as “polluted” remnants. These stars are the dense cores left behind after a Sun‑like star exhausts its nuclear fuel and sheds its outer layers, collapsing into an object roughly the size of Earth but with a mass comparable to the Sun’s. In many cases, the intense gravity of a white dwarf causes heavy elements to sink beneath the visible surface, leaving a pristine hydrogen or helium atmosphere. However, WD J2105‑0722 shows clear spectral lines of sodium, a metal that should have settled out of sight, indicating ongoing accretion of material—likely debris from a disrupted planetary system.

What makes this star truly unique is the way sodium interacts with the star’s light. Sodium atoms absorb photons in the orange portion of the visible spectrum (around 590 nm). When that orange light is removed, the remaining wavelengths combine to produce a faint but discernible greenish glow that can be detected in the star’s spectrum. This “green” signature is not a visual color we would see with the naked eye, but a spectral fingerprint that appears as a distinct dip in the orange band and a relative excess in the green. The effect is analogous to the way sodium street lamps cast a yellow-orange hue on Earth, except on a stellar scale the absorption creates the opposite visual impression.

The presence of sodium in a white dwarf’s atmosphere is itself a rarity. Most polluted white dwarfs exhibit metals such as calcium, iron, and magnesium, which are common in rocky planetary material. Sodium, being more volatile, is typically lost during the intense heating that accompanies the star’s final evolutionary stages. Its detection suggests that the debris feeding the star may be unusually rich in volatile compounds, perhaps originating from icy bodies or comets that survived the star’s red‑giant phase. This hints at a complex, multi‑stage planetary system that endured the cataclysmic transformation of its host star, offering a tantalizing glimpse into the long‑term fate of solar systems like our own.

The find also underscores the power of modern spectroscopic surveys. The team employed the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope equipped with the ESPRESSO instrument, which can resolve minute variations in stellar spectra. By stacking multiple observations and applying sophisticated modeling, the researchers were able to isolate the sodium absorption feature from background noise and confirm its persistence over several months. Such precision opens the door to detecting other subtle chemical anomalies in white dwarfs, potentially revealing a broader diversity of “colored” remnants that have so far gone unnoticed.

Looking ahead, astronomers plan to target a larger sample of white dwarfs with similar high‑resolution techniques, searching for additional cases of sodium or other elements that could produce unusual spectral colors. If more green‑glowing remnants are found, they could redefine classification schemes for stellar remnants and deepen our understanding of planetary system evolution after stellar death. For now, the eerie emerald glow of WD J2105‑0722 serves as a reminder that even in the quiet aftermath of a star’s life, the universe can still surprise us with spectral fireworks—just in time to haunt the night sky this Halloween.
